questions.question: Explain the structure of a history essay.
questions.expected_answer: Introduction: one paragraph answering the question directly with a line of argument and outlining the main points. Body: several paragraphs, each with a topic sentence stating one main point, supporting evidence (facts, dates, names, examples, quotations) and a link back to the question, using linking words. Conclusion: sums up the argument and answers the question again without new information. Written in the past tense, own words, formal language; planned first.

questions.question: Compare the ways of life of the San and the Khoikhoi in the seventeenth century.
questions.expected_answer: San: hunter-gatherers in small mobile family groups; men hunted with bows and poisoned arrows, women gathered most food with digging sticks; rich spiritual beliefs, trance dance and rock art. Khoikhoi: herders of fat-tailed sheep and long-horned cattle (wealth, milk, hides); larger clans/chiefdoms under leaders; seasonal movement with livestock; portable reed-mat huts; traded livestock with ships for copper, iron, beads and tobacco.

questions.question: Why must historians be careful with written sources about the early Cape?
questions.expected_answer: Most written sources (Van Riebeeck's journal, VOC records, travellers' accounts) were written by colonists and show their point of view, interests and prejudices; the voices of the Khoikhoi, San and enslaved people are often missing or distorted. Historians must ask who wrote a source, why and for whom, and use other evidence such as archaeology, rock art and oral traditions.
